results.comparisonNotes: This is a contemporary urban setting in a real-world capital city (Tbilisi, Georgia) with standard institutions: public school, municipal library, bus/metro, neighborhood commerce, and typical apartment living. A general language model is likely to have solid background knowledge of urban post-Soviet/Georgian life at a structural level (apartment blocks, public transit, public schooling, libraries, small shops, budget-conscious households), though it may be weaker on fine-grained local details (exact transit routes, specific school practices, or library policies). Georgian as the main language with growing English exposure, and the presence of Orthodox churches alongside secular institutions, are all well within ordinary-world patterns the model can generalize from. Everyday economy (budgeting, errands, mixed walking/transit mobility) and intellectual access (school curricula, libraries, internet, media) are also standard. Overall, the model can rely on real-world knowledge rather than inventing basic structures, but may still need to approximate some specifically Georgian institutional or cultural nuances.

This setting is a contemporary urban East Asian environment (Kaohsiung, Taiwan) with public schools, mixed-use neighborhoods, scooters, buses, MRT/light rail, convenience stores, markets, and libraries. These are all domains where a general language model is likely to have substantial background knowledge from training data, including Taiwan-specific details at a moderate level of granularity. The household structure (two caregivers plus a cousin, with a nonresident but involved parent) is slightly less stereotypical than a nuclear family but still well within common patterns the model can handle without fabrication. Public schooling, transit, markets, and libraries in Kaohsiung are well-documented online, so everyday routines, institutional procedures, and material circumstances can be described with reasonable confidence. Language use (Mandarin, Taiwanese Hokkien, some English) and the visible mix of religious and secular life are also broadly familiar patterns. The main limitations would be in very fine-grained local practices (specific school rules, exact layout of a given market, or hyperlocal slang), but the overall everyday structure is standard and well-covered, hence consistently high sub-scores rather than a 5 reserved for globally dominant or extremely generic settings.

This setting is in a large, well-documented Brazilian city (Recife) over a contemporary time frame (2004–2026), with ordinary urban conditions: modest apartment living, municipal public school, bus-based mobility, public markets, community learning spaces, and common Brazilian religious and cultural diversity. A general language model is likely to have substantial background knowledge about Brazilian urban life, public schooling, bus systems, feiras, and digital-access initiatives, even if not hyper-local to Casa Amarela. Household structure (single caregiver, siblings, nearby relative) and economic conditions (generally secure food/housing but variable income, reliance on repair/sharing/public services) are also common and well within typical training data. Portuguese as the main language with some English via media and schooling is standard for Brazil, and the listed institutions (municipal school, city bus network, public health, sports/cultural programs) are all familiar types. The only areas where the model might need to interpolate are very specific municipal program details or hyper-local infrastructure, but the everyday structure is broadly covered and does not require fabrication of basic patterns.

This setting is moderately familiar for a general language model. Urban life in a major Moroccan city like Fès, with a mix of newer districts and a historic medina, public schooling, shared taxis/buses, and rail travel, aligns well with widely documented real-world patterns. Household structure (multi-generational apartment, nearby cousins), public services, and modest but stable material circumstances are all common and well-covered in general training data. The multilingual environment (Moroccan Arabic at home, MSA in formal contexts, French in education/administration) is also well-documented, though fine-grained code-switching norms and local slang would require some guessing. Everyday economy (markets, craft workshops, small vendors, tracking discretionary spending) and institutional landscape (public schools, community/digital learning centers, ONCF rail, medina commerce) are broadly known, but specific neighborhood-level routines, exact school practices, and detailed community-program operations are less standardized and would need some fabrication. Intellectual access via TV, internet, religious and secular scholarship, and vocational programs is typical for an urban Moroccan context and reasonably well-covered, though the exact mix and quality of access over 2004–2026 would involve some extrapolation. Overall, the model can rely on substantial real-world background knowledge, with only moderate gaps in local specificity and temporal evolution of services and infrastructure.

This setting is a contemporary, English-speaking, lower-to-middle income household in an Australian state capital, with government schooling, public transport, libraries, and common civic institutions. While Hobart- and Tasmania-specific details (geography, weather patterns, exact transport options, local institutions) are somewhat niche, they are still well-documented and structurally similar to other small Anglophone cities. A general language model will have strong generic templates for rented housing, separated caregivers, public schools, bus-based mobility, and public libraries, and can map these onto Hobart with moderate reliability. It may need to interpolate or guess finer-grained local practices (exact bus routes, school policies, library programs, ferry rollout timeline, specific community clubs), but the everyday structure is very familiar and well within ordinary-world coverage rather than requiring invention from scratch.
